utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Madam, will you please make the solemn declaration in the document which the court usher is giving you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, Madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. On behalf of the Prosecution, I wish to extend the excuses of Mr. Groome, who has lost a family member, his father-in-law, suddenly, and he will not be able to be present, and we will continue with the work of the Prosecution by the other members of the team and in accordance with the rulings made by this Chamber. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Domazet. Examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Neskovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neskovic, before we begin the examination which I will do on behalf of the Defence counsel, I would like to ask you, before answering my question, to wait a few moments. You will also be able to see on the screen the translation, and we wish to facilitate the work of the interpreters and to make sure that both questions and answers are properly and accurately interpreted. I hope that we will be able to complete the examination. I'm sorry that you were called this morning, though that was not planned, as you only arrived last night, but because precisely of what we have just learnt from Mr. Ossogo, certain changes have taken place. I understand that you must be tired, but please do your best so that the proceedings can move forward. First of all, Mrs. Neskovic, will you please introduce yourself. Tell us your first and last name, the place and date of birth, and where you now reside.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Snezana Neskovic. I was born on the 10th of January, 1962, in Sase, in Visegrad municipality. Currently I'm living in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Madam, it's not necessary for to you watch the screen to see if they're keeping up with you. It's only when you have heard the question, wait until the question has finished being typed before you answer. The court reporters are able to keep up with you once you start to speak. It's the interpreters we have a problem with, so if you look at the screen and make sure the question has stopped being typed and then commence your answer. I'm sorry if it wasn't made clear to you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us, Mrs. Neskovic, when and where you were born. Are you married? Do you have children, please, and where does your family live?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I do have a family. I am married. I have a husband and two children, and we all live in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your educational background? What is the highest level of schooling that you have?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: By occupation I am a lawyer. I have a degree in law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are you working now, Mrs. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm working in the local administration of Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neskovic, will you please tell me, after the first multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, were you involved in political life and were you active in Visegrad municipality?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: After the first multi-party elections held on the 20th of November, 1990, I was elected as deputy to the Municipal Assembly of Visegrad, and I participated in the work of the Visegrad Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us on which party's list were you a candidate?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I was on the list of the Serbian Democratic Party, and I was elected deputy on behalf of that party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please check that the questions have been answered before starting -- have been translated before starting your answer. Will you tell us what the balance of forces was in the Municipal Assembly at the time?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the number of deputies in the assembly, according to the parties? I didn't quite understand what you are asking me or are you talking to me about the population?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this case, I am talking about the distribution of forces in the assembly, between the parties, and how the local government was set up after those multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections, the Serbs were in the minority in the Municipal Assembly. The Muslim SDA had the majority in the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, in those days and according to the statute in force at the time, what kind of majority was necessary for a decision to be taken on important issues?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Decision-making on important matters in the assembly, according to the statute in force, a two-thirds majority was required. However, after the multi-party elections, when the SDA party won a majority of seats in the assembly, it undertook to revise the statute, and in an illegal manner, they amended the Municipal Assembly statute, as the Serbs, according to the 1991 census and the previous census of 1981 were in the minority in the Municipal Assembly. The Muslims illegally amended the statute and replaced two-thirds majority into a simple majority for decision-making. The Serbs protested against this amendment of the statute, but this was not endorsed by the president of the assembly so that the statute was voted into force and the dissatisfied Serbs walked out of the second assembly meeting. I think that the statute was amended sometime in 1990 during the second session of the Visegrad Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neskovic, you are saying that this occurred during the second session of the same assembly, the first probably being the constitutive assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that it was amended illegally, was the same two-thirds majority, according to the statute, required for any amendment to the statute, and as such a majority did not exist, that is why you're describing the decision as being unlawful or for some other reason? So would you explain what you mean?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Because for the statute to be amended, a two-thirds majority was required, and according to regulations of the same statute, a public debate had to be held on the statute. However, the president of the Municipal Assembly explained that this would take a lot of time and cost a lot of money to have a public debate, that there hadn't been any public debates before and that the statute would be amended expeditiously, at the same session of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Fikret Cocalic, a graduate lawyer who represented the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please wait a couple of minutes after my question, because you are answering them very quickly again. Will you please tell us, Mrs. Neskovic, what were the effects of what you have just told us on the continued work of the assembly and the bodies of the Visegrad Municipal Assembly in which you were employed?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: This had a negative impact on the work of the Municipal Assembly in Visegrad. The Muslims grabbed all the power for themselves. The president of the Municipal Assembly was from the SDA. The president of the executive council was from the SDA, and Muslims also held other important positions. The president of the court was a Muslim. The president of the magistrate's court was a Muslim. The public prosecutor was a Muslim. The chief of the public security station was also a Muslim. Only some minor positions were left to the Serbs, which were of very little significance. The Serbs got the positions of the vice-president of the assembly. This was a honourary post. The person was not fully employed in the Municipal Assembly. To appease the Serbs, a position was more or less invented, the position of the vice-president of the executive council to which a Serb had been appointed, and until those elections, such a position had not existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neskovic, you said yourself that according to the census results, the Serbs were in the minority to both of the previous censuses. So I'd like to know, before this assembly session in which you were a deputy, how was authority shared in Visegrad before?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Before this assembly session, the method of decision-making was different. The government was formed in a different manner, because election laws were written for the elections -- the first multi-party elections in 1990. Before those elections, the Serbs held one-third of the power according to the statute. For instance, if the president of the Municipal Assembly was a Muslim, the president of the executive council or government had to be a Serb and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I call this system of distribution of positions to all the positions of authority in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The same key was applied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period when this key was implemented, were there any problems in the functioning of the local authorities and the government and the assembly in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neskovic, when you say you don't remember or don't know, does that mean that you don't remember any problems, any particular problems, and that you would remember if there had been any special problems?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: There were problems after the Second World War. At the end of the Second World War, the Serbs started moving out of Visegrad municipality en masse because of the Chetnik movement. Many of them could not find employment, so many went to Serbia and abroad. There was a local community called Zabrdzje consisting of 10.000 people from Visegrad and Rogatica, whereas the Muslims who mostly supported the Ustasha movement and the NDH, the independent Croatian state, the border of which was the Drina and extended as far as Zemun, later switched sides and joined the Partizans. The Partizan movement was very slow in -- was very small in the Visegrad area, whereas the Serbs supported the Chetnik movement to save their lives, and that was the reason why the Serbs mostly moved out. And the Zabrdzje community was set up in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're talking about the period immediately after the Second World War. Does that mean to say that many Serbs from Visegrad and the environs settled this area around Obrenovac that you mentioned, some 10.000 people? Do you mean that they lived there then or now?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: They live there now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For those of us who may not understand, would you explain what you mean by the NDH, what state you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the independent State of Croatia, which was a fascist entity set up on the 10th of April, 1941, the leader of which was Ante Pavlevic. And the policy toward the Serbs was that a third should be killed, a third converted to Catholicism, and a third expelled. And the worst suffering was along the Drina River, because that state -- that state's borders were along the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're getting no translation of either the question or the answer, I'm afraid. I think you better ask the question again, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat the question because it was omitted from the transcript. So please wait a moment. When you mentioned the NDH government which extended as far as the Drina River and the Chetnik movement, were the two opposed to one another, that is, the Chetnik movement and the NDH forces, or were they allies?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: They were opposed to one another. They were not allies. The Chetniks took part in the struggle against the NDH because they were defending the Serb people. Since with the establishment of the NDH in April 1941, massive liquidation and expulsion of Serbs started, especially along the left bank of the Drina, because certain families were totally wiped out and exterminated. In order to protect themselves from such misdeeds by the Muslims who immediately joined the Ustasha movement, the Serbs formed the Chetnik movement to protect Serb villages and the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I think we should move 50 years on, don't you? This is well-known history. Let's get on to the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question, because talking to you, I know that you studied this. So I just have one question for you regarding the population structure in Visegrad. You mentioned 1991 and 1981. Could you tell us very briefly how the population composition developed according to the censuses that we -- that you studied. Did the share of Serbs go down in relation to the Muslim population and when or, rather, do you have information as to when the Serbs were in the majority in that area?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Censuses in Visegrad municipality were carried out several times in the period from 1895 until 1991. According to the censuses up to 1971 in Visegrad municipality, the Serbs were in the majority. It is after 1971 that the Serbs became a minority in Visegrad municipality. According to the 1991 census, there were 82.8 per cent Muslims and 32.3 per cent Serbs in Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's something wrong there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Something is wrong. I shall ask. But she said -- I think that is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be a mistake in the percentages, because it's more than 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 68.3. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So according to data available to you, you said that until 1971, the Serbs were in the majority. But you also said that many had emigrated before that so that the majority was declining up to 1971 to become a minority then.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it means. The Serbs moved out because they couldn't find jobs, and they went to areas where they could find employment. And also because of the policies that were implemented toward Serbs after the Second World War. That is why the number of Serbs declined at the census of 1971. Another reason was that the Muslims became a majority in 1971 because until 1971, Muslims were considered an ethnic group. However, for the 1971 census, they became a nation in 1967. And it is only in 1971 that they could declare their nationality to be Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us go back to 1990 or, rather, the period from 1990 to 1992, when you were a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Visegrad. You told us that already at the second session this amendment to the statute was made and that the Serb deputies walked out of the assembly. When you told us that, did they leave that session and come back the next time or did they not come back at all? Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs came back to the Municipal Assembly hoping that the situation would improve, and they did take part in the subsequent Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sessions. However, the situation remained unchanged more or less. Until the end of 1991, the Serbs took part in the work of the Visegrad Municipal Assembly. However, at the third assembly session, in spite of the Serbs' opposition, who were supposed to propose candidates to certain positions, the Muslims proposed Serbs married to Muslims, and the Serbs never recognised those appointments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said this, madam, would you explain why they did not approve? Was it because they didn't consider them capable for those positions or because they were married to Muslim women?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs felt that they should be the ones to appoint candidates to those positions and not the SDA. They were not the candidates chosen by the Serbs. And not because their wives were Muslim but to create the impression that the Serbs were participating in government, the Muslims proposed those particular Serbs to those positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neskovic, since you were elected deputy on the list of the Serbian Democratic Party, I assume that you were a member of that party, and I'm asking you: Were you a member of that party?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember which party was formed first prior to the multi-party elections when multi-partiness was introduced into Yugoslav life?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The first party that was established in Visegrad was the Democratic Action Party, and it was established, I think two or three months before the Serbian Democratic Party, SDS. The founding meeting of the SDA was held in what was then the cultural centre building, and it was attended by many people including Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the party at the time, and Sulejman Ugljanin was, I guess, the president of the SDA for Sandzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sandzak is in Serbia; is that right, Mrs. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the first promotions that this party had and meetings? Were there any incidents that took place or anything that could have disturbed the rest of the population?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the Muslims had organised themselves first, two three months later, the Serbs set up the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, and the founding meeting of the party was held at the sports centre of Usce, and it was well frequented for the most part by the rural population, whereas the SDA was supported by practically all the Muslims. The newly established SDS was mostly supported by the rural population, whereas the urban population did not state its views. But they preferred the SDP, Nijaz Durakovic who held the SDP. However, after his statement that he made to the effect that the scent of incense threatened to stifle us, the Serb population voted for the SDS held on the 20th of November 1990. Immediately after its founding provocations on the part of the Muslims started. Slogans began to be written up on the facades of houses and buildings. It said "Long live the SDA. The SDS will be blown away. The SDS will wear a fez," that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the two parties that were established, the SDA as a Muslim party and the SDS as a Serb party, and you also mentioned one other party, the SDP. Could you give us the full name of the SDP party and tell us whether at the time it represented a multi-ethnic party or not.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The socialist democratic party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the president of which was Nijaz Durakovic. In fact, it was a transformation of the League of Communists. The League of Communists became the SDP party prior to the multi-party elections, and this pre-electoral meeting for the party was held at the sports centre of Usce, and it was perhaps the most people rallied to it. There were more people attending that meeting than the SDN/SDS party meeting, but at the elections the party fared very badly. I can't remember the precise figures, but I don't think it got more than two deputies. All those who supported that party up until then voted predominantly either for the SDS or for the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say, Mrs. Neskovic, that the party had a lot of supporters in Visegrad and you would say that there were even more people at their promotion meeting than at the others. Tell me, please, at the time when it had supporters, were they -- and sympathisers, were they both Serbs and Muslims or just one and just the other?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The founding meeting, pre-electoral founding meeting, was attended by both nations, and it was the League of Communists that had become transformed to the Social Democratic Party. And the rule was before the multi-party elections in 1990, that if for example the president of the committee was a Serb, the secretary had to be a Muslim or vice versa. Is that what you meant? I'm not sure I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I wonder how far we have to go into this. It's not really an issue, is it? We've got the history. Perhaps not as well expressed as this witness has put it, but we've got this history in evidence pretty well. If you want her to develop something, by all means, take the witness to it, but we really do have this pretty well documented, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. I shall try and abridge that portion and wind that up by asking several more questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neskovic, you mentioned the president of the party, probably for the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you said his name was Nijaz Durakovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any significant function in the previous League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and what nationality was he?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He was a Muslim by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you mentioned him making a statement which, in your opinion, led to the fact that many Serbs who were in favour of the party did not actually vote for it, and you mentioned a word that he used, that the smell of incense was expanding. Did I understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the meeting he said that the smell of incense threatened to stifle us, not that it was expanding, and he was referring to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is incense something that is used in the lithogies [phoen] of the Serbian Orthodox Church and that that is why it is associated with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These incense are used during religious customs of the Serbs either at home or in church, and these incense are petrified resin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neskovic, after those elections the party that represented a multi-ethnic one and used to be the League of Communist of Yugoslavia at the Visegrad elections fared very well -- fared very poorly. Interpreter's correction -- and did the election results reflect the percentage of the population, the Serbs and Muslims in Visegrad, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The electoral results did reflect the state of affairs in the -- according to the population census in the Visegrad municipality as far as I recall, but don't hold me to my word. One or two deputies of the 31 deputies and 50 deputies that the Municipal Assembly of Visegrad had were Muslims and 19 deputies were Serbs. So 31 and 19 of the 50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neskovic, you took part as a deputy yourself on behalf of the Serbian Democratic Party, and you said that the Serb deputies did return after the third meeting. What happened next? Did the situation improve in some way? And how did local government function in future, in view of what you said?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The situation did not improve at all, on the contrary. It deteriorated with each passing day. Excessive incidents occurred in town which were a threat to peace, and particularly active in that were the Sabanovic brothers, Murat and Avdija. And Avdija was a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Visegrad. The Municipal Assembly very often, after the outbreak of these incidents and events which threatened to upset peace discussed the matters but the conclusions were never respected, and the information that was pouring in from the public security stations were very scant. After the establishment of the SDA and the victory at the multi-party elections, there was a general euphoria on the part of the Muslims led by the Sabanovic brothers. They began intercepting Serbs in town, destroying the monuments, stopping the convoys of the then Yugoslav People's Army and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, among other things, the destruction of monuments. Can you tell us briefly about an incident like that that occurred?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that sometime in mid-June - I can't remember the exact date - that the monument to Ivo Andric was destroyed on the Visegrad square and this was done by Murat Sabanovic and his group. That everything was organised could be seen from the fact that the actual act of destroying the monument was filmed. Fadil Hajdarevic, who was the proprietor of a videotech at the time filmed the destruction of the monument, and you could view the tapes around town. They could be found. Murat had destroyed the monument, and the head of the sculpture was thrown into the Drina River. All of this was followed by the statement of Muhamed Filiopovic Tunjo, the president of the MDO, who said that Andric did more harm to the Muslims than all the armies that passed through Bosnia. That triggered off the destruction of the monument to my mind and also an article which appeared in a Sarajevo daily which wrote negative comments about writer Andric. And on the title page there was a picture of the author himself impaled on a pen which symbolised the impaling of Serbs by the Turks and this was described in Ivo Andric's novel -- famous novel, the bridge on the Drina, the impaling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neskovic, you mention add moment ago some graffiti that appeared in town and led to the disquiet of the population. Could you tell us what the graffiti expressed and why they led to these feelings of disquiet amongst the population?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: They were written in oil -- green oil paint which is -- green is considered to be a Muslim colour, and they were visibly written up on the buildings of the forestry administration of the Visegrad municipality and the Panos company. It said "SDA democracy, SDA -- SDS, you will wear a fez. Serbs, get out and move to Serbia." That was written up, and it was very ugly, on the facades of the buildings, and it caused the Serbs to be afraid. And the director of the firm who was a Muslim had to have the building repainted, a new facade to cover up the graffiti although you could still see the remains of the graffiti underneath the new facade and paint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that one of the graffiti said "Serbs, go to Serbia." And did this actually happen? Did the citizens of Visegrad start to leave Visegrad or did they not?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, people did leave because of the fear, because of the provocations that were continuous. The Serbs felt jeopardised, especially the women and children, and they began to take refuge by moving to Serbia. And prior to the outbreak of the conflict in 1992, I think that in the town there were very few Serbs left, only about a hundred, and that everybody who could fled to the surrounding villages or to Serbia proper, and I myself fled to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you want to say that you, too, in the face of what was happening, left Visegrad and moved to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I left Visegrad, and through the village of Jelasica I fled to Uzice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that happen? When was that, Mrs. Neskovic, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was perhaps the day before the dam was released or, rather, the water on the hydroelectric power plant by Murat Sabanovic. Towards evening, that is when we fled from our house to the mezzanine settlement which is a part of Visegrad. And while we were fleeing, the shooting had already started and we fled with these incendiary bullets and the first Serb houses were set on fire. So it was a matter of saving our heads. First of all, the first Serb, Mico Indic lost his life and Serb houses were set afire. Zoran Pecikoza and Miso Savic's house. So there was one man killed and these two houses set alight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you repeat whose houses were burnt? I don't think it was translated.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb houses. Zoran Pecikoza's house and Miso Savic's house. One was in the Mahala district, and the other was in the Glavica district. You could see the smoke coming out of those houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, when you left Visegrad, perhaps only a hundred Serbs were left in Visegrad proper, and when you spoke of that hundred, is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A small number, a much smaller number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [no translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we've lost the interpretation again. You have to ask your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Only when you said that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone was on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's something desperately wrong with this set, I'm afraid. We heard none of what Mr. Domazet said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neskovic, once you left Visegrad and fled to Serbia, did you ever return, and if so, when to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I returned at the end of the April, once the Uzice Corps had entered, because the Uzice Corps, when it entered Visegrad, called upon all the inhabitants of Visegrad, Muslims and Serbs alike, to return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to what you remember, this appeal from the Uzice Corps, was it fruitful? Did most of the Serbs and Muslims in fact return to Visegrad after this appeal was launched?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the Serbs did return, as far as I remember, whereas a smaller number of Muslims returned. But the vast majority did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell us, Mrs. Neskovic, about that period while the Uzice Corps was in Visegrad? Were there any significant incidents? Did the factories and companies function? What was it like during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were no untoward incidents. Everybody was called up for their work assignment, to respond, and the town itself, as far as I remember, the shops were destroyed, the shop windows were broken so that the goods were left open, but people started putting back windows, restoring the glass, and people went round to see what had been looted and what needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The appeal for the return of the Serbs to Visegrad was also an appeal for everybody to go back to their work posts, their jobs?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time, were the factories and companies working, the ones which had worked up until then?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the conditions and circumstances had changed. Some of the companies had been damaged when the water was released from the hydroelectric power plant. All the goods had been taken away, and so an inventory had to be taken to see what was lacking so that the production process could be restored and organised again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neskovic, where were you yourself working before you went to Uzice and then returned? Where did you work as a legal person?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in the Varda Visegrad timber industry, and I was a clerk for property relations, property and legal relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact that you were a deputy in the assembly, that was not your professional -- professional paid function, it was just a political function; is that right? But you worked in the Varda company. Is that what I understand?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned damage done by the release of the dam, the water of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the dam. Can you tell us something about that dam incident? You said that you yourself had left Visegrad just before that happened, so you probably know something about it or heard about it anyway.

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about it over the media, over the radio, actually. I heard that Murat Sabanovic had released the water at the hydroelectric power plant of Visegrad, and afterwards, when I returned from Uzice, from being a refugee there, I saw what the water done, where the water had flooded. For example, in my particular district it had flowed out onto the street itself so that all the trees were blocking the road. I saw freight vehicles that had been overturned by the banks from the force of the water. And when I went to the Varda company, my company, and in that district it was in the hydroelectric power plant district, I saw that the water had taken away the whole road and the little houses that were inhabited by the Muslims, because Uzice is a Muslim settlement predominantly. And these houses behind the factory had been damaged as well and several of them swept away by the water. The water had also swept away the bridge which linked this settlement with the opposite bank the Drina and the Nezuci settlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to what you learnt and heard at that time, this release of water from the dam, was all the water released from the dam or was it just partially released?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to learn from the media, it was the partial release of water, because Murat Sabanovic wanted to release all the water from the dam, but according to his own words, someone -- a corps closed off the valves. I don't understand the process, but I know that not all the water from the dam was released. Had all the water flowed out of the dam, I think there would be nothing left of Visegrad practically, because we saw marks of the -- how high the water came on the town. So had all the water from the dam been released, the whole of the town would have been flooded, and there were blue marks left where the level of the water was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that your own settlement was in jeopardy. Are you now talking about the part you live in now? You have your own family. Or were you referring to the part of town where you lived before you were married?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: That the -- all the water from the dam had been released, as far as I was informed, the whole town would have been destroyed. However, only part of the water was released so that the water destroyed -- the closest district was Dusce, which was by the hydroelectric power plant, close by, Dusce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, don't you think we've had enough of this already. We've got most of this evidence in and there's been no dispute about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have concluded that portion, and my next question to you, Mrs. Neskovic is: Did you know Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you known him?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Mr. Vasiljevic has or, rather, had a private house a kilometre further off from where I lived with my parents. So to all intents and purposes, we lived in the same street. But he was one kilometre further up, and my parents' house was further down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the house he lived in was approximately one kilometre away from your parents' house where you lived before you were married; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long he had been living in that house that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly. Perhaps ten years or four or five years before the war broke out. He had built it -- been building it. I know that he worked in the Panos company as a waiter. The Panos company is a catering establishment and company in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him as a waiter? Did you see him when he was working as a waiter?

utterances.speaker: SNEZANA NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, it's just on 11.00. I am very concerned that the doctor that we started off with last night be allowed to get away, and as soon as Ms. Bauer is ready to take up that particular witness, I think we should return to him because he did talk about some patients waiting for him to return for him to operate on them. So as soon as Ms. Bauer is ready to deal with him, I think we should be told, and we'll get that doctor out of the way before we -- before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you would like, after the break, if Mrs. Bauer is ready, we can continue with the witness Jovanovic. I think that we will be able to complete him, because I don't have too many questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. As I understand it, his evidence goes to only two very simple or short issues, whether the accused was there and the nature of his conduct at the time, and that shouldn't take very long one hopes, but I just want that doctor kept here over the weekend so his that patients are still waiting for their operations. Perhaps you can make some inquiries of Ms. Bauer as to when she'll be ready and if she is ready at 11.30, we'll go on with him then. We will adjourned now until 11.30

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Doctor, you have been kept waiting, but I am assured that you will be away from here today. Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Domazet: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Jovanovic, we shall continue with what we started yesterday. If you remember -- you have a problem. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I was saying, Mr. Jovanovic, that we will continue what we started yesterday. You explained the situation in your hospital at the time in 1992 at the Uzice hospital. I should like to ask you, in view of the fact that at the time you were a young doctor in terms of experience, did you have a mentor, a more experienced doctor who worked with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had a mentor. It is customary and obligatory. It was the late Primarius Dr. Stanisavljevic. He was my mentor, and in a sense, he was responsible for everything I did. He died on the 23rd of January, 1996, just after I had sat for my specialist examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Jovanovic, in view of that, did you still have your own patients that you treated independently, as did the other doctors that were on specialist training?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. This is regulated not only by our own internal regulations but by the law. I had no right to what one might call my own patients. That expression, "personal patients," is use for practical reasons. Every specialist has rooms to which patients were admitted that he admitted during his shift on duty or work in the outpatient clinic. On Mondays I would do the rounds in my department. And this is being done still. And on other days, in the so-called small block to which the room in which the patient, because of whom we are here today, was hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I ask you about your rounds, let me also ask you whether at the time you could be the doctor on duty at night, because there was always someone on duty at night in your department, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. I would be on duty as the so-called junior duty doctor, and I would cover all injuries that could be treated in the operations room for minor surgeries, within the framework of the admissions department of the hospital. Of course, at the same time I performed my regular duties in my original department, the department I belonged to, the orthopedics department, where one doctor specialist was on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talking about the rounds, could you clarify for us what this weekly round meant? Was it together with other doctors, visiting the patients in your departments, and what you mean when you said you visited the small block, as you called it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Mondays we have the large morning rounds made together with the head of the department. All doctors, the head nurse of the department, and the other responsible nurses, we visit all the patients in the orthopedics ward. On the other days, the rounds are made separately. Each doctor visits his own rooms. In those days, each specialist had three rooms to care for. And as I was an intern in that department, I would attend the rounds being made in one of the units of our department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I go into the specifics, let me ask you something about Dr. Jovicevic. What was his position in the general hospital at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days he was the deputy director of the general hospital, and at the same time, he performed the duties of a specialist in the department. He reduced his obligations in the outpatients clinic because he simply couldn't manage to cover all those things because of his obligations as the director. Occasionally he was on duty, and that's what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether in those days he had a political function of any kind in the municipality in Uzice, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember. I'm not able to tell you exactly what the post was, but in our mutual conversations, we referred to him as belonging to the ruling and then only party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were speaking about your obligations, making rounds and visiting patients of a particular block and patients in general, in view of the number of patients you had, what was the rough figure for the whole department, if you can remember? Of course I'm referring to 1992, the middle of 1992.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The department has 60 beds. When I said that we were fully booked, I would say on an average, 75 per cent of the beds were occupied. And in those days and the days that followed, the occupancy rate went up to 100 per cent, which meant all 60 beds. And sometimes even patients, whose injuries allowed, it would be transferred to the neighbouring department which did -- was not so overcrowded, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that sometimes there was such pressure that patients had to be accommodated in other rooms, in rooms of other departments?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what that means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, you said that it was a large hospital, a regional hospital, and that it covered patients from a rather large region before the conflict and during the conflict. So in addition to civilians, would it admit also people from the military?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say, military men? I would see them in uniform, patients in uniform and patients without uniform. What was important for me and my colleagues and what was their common denominator were their injuries. So to answer your question, yes, there were military men among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put the question differently. In the territory around the town of Uzice, was there a military hospital of any kind, an exclusively military hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that our hospital looked like a military hospital in those days, and I am not aware that there were any other hospitals of that kind, because we admitted, as part of our regular duties, all the injured from that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know, Doctor, where in Serbia there are military hospitals, in which towns there are military hospitals today and whether that was the case at the time? Of course, if you know.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did my regular military service in Nis, and for a time I was hospitalised there in a military hospital. So I know there was one there in Nis. And I also know of the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade. I cannot remember any others. But in any case, if there are any others, they're certainly not of that scale as these two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That is quite right. They are the two military hospitals. Could we say for the record what is the rough distance between Uzice and Nis, and Uzice and Belgrade? Is it the distance more or less the same? What is it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I frequently travel along that route. It is 200 kilometres to Belgrade, 210, 220. I drive my own car. And to Nis it's about 10 or 20 kilometres more than that, than the distance to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, when you were a young doctor at the Uzice hospital, in this department, do you remember Mitar Vasiljevic as a patient?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do remember is the atmosphere that developed around patient Vasiljevic, and I can also state that I remember the Vasiljevic case. If I were to say anything else, it would be a misinterpretation of those events. Of course I have refreshed some of those memories over the past few weeks when this case aroused more interest, and I did so exclusively talking to my colleagues at the department. As far as the face is concerned, I'm afraid I wouldn't recognise him if I were to see him in an elevator, never mind anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Dr. Jovanovic, you said that you remember something specific about that period. Tell us what it is you remember. You said that it's not his face, but do you remember something from those days?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What attracted my attention was a patient who disturbed the order by his behaviour, the house rules. I remember the way in which he was injured, by falling from a horse. I had expected all kinds of causes of injury from that area but not this, because it was something quite unusual, out of the ordinary, and of course, it is not customary for our patient to be transferred to the psychiatric ward. For this there had to be a reason, and the reason existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Jovanovic, that is what you remember about that period, though you told us that you wouldn't recognise the face even today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this behaviour of his that you have described mentioned during the rounds or did you hear about it in some other way? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I participated in the rounds and visits to that room, I would hear the briefing of the responsible nurse of that unit of our department who would convey what she had to say, probably what she had heard from the other patients lying in the same room with him. So in any event, I know about it indirectly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Jovanovic, when you mentioned your duties in those days, making rounds, and you said that Mondays were the days for the major rounds when you visited all the patients and on other days you only visited patients in one particular block to which you were assigned. Was Mitar Vasiljevic a patient in that block or would you see him only once a week during the big rounds?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in a room belonging to the part of the department which I would tour every day except if I had a free day or if it was my weekend off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to look at an exhibit, please, and to comment on it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at P138. Could it be shown to the witness, please, in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look carefully at this document and then I will have some questions for you about it. Will you please tell me, Mr. Jovanovic, do you recognise this document as a document from your hospital in those days? You have the case history in front of you. Is that the case history of the patient you referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the customary document, a case history with the entries made in the same way that we're doing it today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this same printed form used today for case histories?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is in use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the first page and the top right-hand corner where it says the number of the case history and the date -- below that, the date of admission. My question is: Does the date of admission have to reflect the date when the patient was indeed admitted?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it must. Anything else would be incorrect. That date indicates the date the patient was admitted to hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that date entered according to the hour of arrival? Does it cover that day until midnight? And if the patient arrives after 2400 hours, then the following date is noted down?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the practice as the admission service works 24 hours, round the clock, so this date means that on that day up to midnight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the number of the case history that is indicated in the same right-hand corner, could another patient be given the came number if he were a patient in another hospital department?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This personal number is an identification number, and it is unique for each patient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it attributed to patients in the order in which they are admitted or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. That is the only logical way to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you that, I meant that at the beginning of the year, the first patient is attributed number 1 and then it goes on in order until the end of the year. Was that the procedure?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at the top left-hand corner of this case history and what has been typewritten there. Would you read it, please, and could you tell us what that information is as it doesn't -- it isn't part of the form itself but has been typed on top of the regular columns? Do you know what it means?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the top left-hand corner, in handwriting is the room number, and in the right-hand corner the initials of the doctor admitting the patient. For purely practical reasons, so that the nurses who actually take the patient to a bed, that they should know which room they should put him in. That is the room of the orthopaedist who admitted him. Then it says that the SUP has been informed. That means that the admissions department informed the competent authorities, in this case the police. Below that it is typewritten that an injury was incurred in the theatre of operations in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, should we be told whose initials those are, the orthopaedist who admitted him?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you mentioned that at the top of the page are the initials of the doctor who admitted the patient. Could you tell us exactly where those initials are and what the letters are?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those initials are to be found in the top right-hand corner, above the printed columns, and the initials are of Dr. Jovicevic. Neither then nor now do we have any other doctor with the same initials. So without any doubt, it was he. This does not mean to say that this has to be his handwriting. I am saying this for purely practical reasons. These initials may be written by the junior doctor or the doctor himself who admitted him. In any event, those are his initials, the first letter of his first name and then the first letter of his surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The letters that you see, are they written in the Cyrillic script or the Latin script, although the J is the same in both scripts, but could you look at both those initials and tell us?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is "DJ".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And it is written in pencil, is it not, not typed out?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the top left-hand corner, also outside the printed columns that exist on the form, would you read out -- does it say from the theatre of operations or battlefield in Visegrad? Could you tell us how the term "battlefield" "Ratiste" was used in sphere of your work? What did the battlefield or theatre of operations mean?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the term battlefield in practice was used as a concept denoting the territory, and the characteristics of that territory was the war atmosphere that prevailed in it. And not as a relevant piece of information indicating exclusively that the injury was inflicted through weapons or combat operations and explosive device or similar things. Looking back from this point in time, we can see, or, rather, I can see that there has been some imprecision as to how we used that particular term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, Dr. Jovanovic, that the term in your records was used to describe every case of an injured person coming from the war zone, regardless of whether he -- the injury was self-inflicted by accident from a firearm or whether he fell and received an injury? What was important for you was that he was coming from the war zone for you to use this term in this place?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging from my own practice, when I took down the basic information upon a patient's admission, my colleagues and I did not give much thought or pay attention to the circumstances in which an injury was caused. What we felt was that it was -- that was up to the relevant and competent authorities, and this is documented by the fact that the police was informed. And I see this in the top left-hand corner. So as surgeons or future surgeons, at that time weren't interested -- it wasn't essential for us to look at that kind of information, and just some war injuries have specific features and characteristics, and it is important to know for further treatment. In this particular case, it was a closed fracture of the lower leg. And for me, as a future orthopaedic surgeon and today as a specialist orthopaedic surgeon, is treated the same way regardless of the cause, regardless of whether the injury was caused by falling off a tank or a haystack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. May we just go back to the doctor's initials for a moment? This was an internal way of establishing which doctor it was. Does that mean that Dr. Jovicevic had his own patients and that Mitar Vasiljevic was one of Dr. Jovicevic's patients? Does that emerge from what you have said?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Perhaps the term "personal patient" is not the best of terms. They are all patients of the Republic of Serbia. But as I say, for practical purposes, we use the term loosely to make matters easier and facilitate our daily work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did each of those doctors, the ones you mentioned, did they have a certain number of beds and rooms allotted to his own personal patients, the patients he was in charge of?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you take a look at that same case history that you have before you and tell us, please, something about the top half and the information contained there? Do you know where those facts are filled in?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That information is filled in at the admissions department of the general hospital. The administrative staff, when they are on duty, fill out the form, the nurse in the admissions department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The hospital admission department, is it one single admissions department for the whole hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The admissions and receptions department is the only one and caters to the whole hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is at the admissions department that they decide where they're going to send the patient, and they fill in the form of the case history. Did I read you correctly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have heard that at the admissions department, doctors from other departments, especially surgeons and orthopaedists, would be on duty. Now, as you were a young doctor at the time, were you one of the doctors who would be on duty from time to time there or did you have nothing to do with the admission of patients?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the prevailing conditions at that time, there was a special regime of organisation and work distribution at the admissions department, which in practical terms meant that we organised an admissions and triage team or teams. That meant that -- actually most of the injuries required a multi-disciplinary approach, that is to say, observation by different specialists from different branches of medicine. And for that reason, we set up teams of this kind. And I myself, as a young surgeon, had a place on them. I was in charge of the lesser injuries, looking after people with less serious injuries, or in certain cases I would assist my senior colleagues in the operations theatre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Jovanovic, would you take a look at that first page of the case history once again, please, and after those first data we have the other columns. Do you notice any columns which are there but have not been filled in?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I had to find something, in the column after treatment, it does not say that the patient, under number 5, was transferred to another department, but let me state that to the present day, at least I myself do not attach great importance to that column because in the majority of cases, I skip it anyway. The discharge sheet contains sufficient information, so sometimes I consider this, personally, to be unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Jovanovic, that piece of information, and you said that you remember a patient that had been transferred to the psychiatric ward, is that piece of information to be found anywhere in the case history? Could you take a look at the rest of the pages, please?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to my own memories, I see that from the document that the patient was transferred to another department within our hospital, and that was the psychiatric department and ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you go back to the first page now, please, once again. I think there's another column which has not been filled in which relates to the date or time of injury. Am I right in saying that? Have you found that column which has not been filled in?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right. And an explanation for that would be the same as for the previous one. Of course, it is not a justification. As we had a great deal of work to contend with during that period, I think it was quite right for us to skip some administrative work, and at the time, we weren't able -- we couldn't have known that they might be important one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer. Cross-examined by Ms. Bauer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Jovanovic. My name is Bauer, and I'm going to ask you several questions on behalf of the Prosecution today. Dr. Jovanovic, am I correct in assuming that today you can't tell us precisely whether you have been on duty when the patient Mitar Vasiljevic was admitted to the hospital or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you also told us that at times you were assigned to the triage of people in the admissions session, and am I correct that then also you filled out some of the medical information in the case history?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct, but in cases when the primary injury was -- came under the competencies of the orthopaedist, that means if it was an injury to the extremities, to the spine, and the patient's life wasn't directly threatened, patients of that kind were admitted to the orthopaedic department. And their particulars, within the frameworks of the case history, I sometimes took down too. That was part of the work that we junior doctors on duty did in the place of the specialists, the othopaedists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look again at the document in front of you, the case history, Exhibit 138, you told us about -- that in the left upper right corner the police was informed. I'm sure you know what "VP" means and stands for, do you, Doctor, at those times?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "VP" is for that period -- at that period of time probably meant the military police, but the piece of information that -- where it says "SUP informed," is the same term we use today if the injuries require that service to be notified, are such that that service should be notified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in this case it means that the military police of the SUP was informed; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time and today too, I'm not acquainted with their internal organisation, whether they have a department for military conscripts, civilians, or whatever. But I am certain that this piece of information - and I told you who filled that in - that it is sent to a telephone number, as far as I know. I can't help you any more than having said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at that time, Doctor, you said that you were there. Would it be usual to inform anybody who came from that region, including women, children, et cetera, would it be usual to inform the military police that a casualty was brought into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every serious bodily injury exists in classification form, and we're duty-bound to inform the relevant police service regardless of where the patient comes from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying then that if a woman would have come from Visegrad theatre, the theatre of battle, as you told us, that also the military police in Visegrad would have been informed at that time of her injury?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, I did not go to Bosna or Visegrad at all, so I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, that's not what I mean. You told us that the term "battlefield" was widely used for people, patients being admitted from Eastern Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question simply was, did this apply to all patients including women?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if you have to inform the police station of such injuries, then it would be your statement that also for women coming from this area the military police would have been informed; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't part of my work, to inform the police. It was the job of the admissions department. I see no reason why somebody should inform the police if a pregnant woman, for example, came from the battle zone, battlefield. So when we said "battlefield," we had in mind the territory, the war zone, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it probably more a fact that you had a military patient in front of you and this is why the military police would be informed and not anybody else?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my job to identify the type of injury and to provide secondary surgical treatment, as we call it. And another service dealt with identification of that kind. It didn't come under my job. All patients for me were the same, similarly important and equal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Jovanovic. If you look at the second page of the case history, please. Now, I'm correct that Dr. Jovicevic most likely Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. filled out the second part of this case history; right? On the top, right on the top.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. And this is not customary for him. He preferred to have the younger doctors do it. And I'm sure that he did this, which is different from the next paragraph which was filled out by the person that conducted the surgical intervention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now could it --

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's not part of your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. So Dr. Jovicevic or a younger doctor, under his instruction filled out these parts; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He filled it out and he typed it out and signed it. I recognise his style because he does it rarely, so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I also correct that you as a trainee doctor at times also filled out such type of -- type of anamnesis, I think it's called?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the doctor please be asked to approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, could move your seat up a little closer to the table. The interpreters are having difficulty hearing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. At that time, most of those anamnesis were written by myself and my younger colleagues, and it is an unfortunate habit of us doctors that we tend to give this type of work to younger doctors. But this particular anamnesis was typed out personally by Dr. Jovicevic. It's not that -- I recognise his style. I wouldn't have to look at the signature or have a fingerprint there, but I know his style very well because I trained under him as a younger colleague, and that's why I am able to recognise his particular style.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your experience, if a patient comes in and he is full conscious, you would ask him, "Well, how did this injury happen?" Correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if somebody were to tell you, "Well, you know, Doctor, I fell off a horse and broke my leg," you would note this down in this record, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. And I try to this day, in my work, not to be an investigator but to trust people, especially when that is not a relevant piece of information for the method of treatment that I plan to prescribe and administer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the patient would tell you, "I fell from a horse and broke it," you would type in this anamnesis that he fell off a horse, injured or broke his leg, fell off a horse?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me when I say that is so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, then, you would agree with me, Doctor, wouldn't you, that the anamnesis written down by Dr. Jovicevic is rather imprecise if Mr. Vasiljevic were to have told him he fell off a horse; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that the anamnesis is not precise, but it is not in contradiction with what I said, because for us, the important thing is whether it is an open fracture or a closed fracture, et cetera, whether the patient fell from a height of 5 metres or 1 metre. Those circumstances are essential. But I do agree with you that the anamnesis could have been more precise, written with greater precision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then the conclusion is obvious that Mr. Vasiljevic probably did not tell the doctor that he fell off a horse, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. That is not an obvious conclusion for me. Perhaps Dr. Jovicevic overlooked the importance of that particular piece of information, and quite honestly, I don't see a great deal of importance of that piece of information except if you look at the event through the prism of the developments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Jovicevic -- Jovanovic, I'm sorry, you are an orthopaedic surgeon. How long usually is the diagnosis of fractura cruris would require that the patient is in traction, or first, is it required that the patient is in traction?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Traction is one of the methods that in Anglo-Saxon literature is hard to fine. It is considered outdated and a brutal method, but in countries such as mine it is frequently applied, and it has its full value in practice. It implies skeletal traction whereby in a slow and safe way the bone is returned to a correct position with the help of this traction apparatus and weights amounting to 10 per cent of bodily weight, roughly, for the duration, roughly, of up to three weeks. And that is the answer to your question. Without any risk of injuring any other blood vessels or nerves or any other important structures of the body. The method allows daily monitoring, X-ray examinations and controls. And the most important thing is to avoid surgery, which under the best of circumstances, has its risks. The method is applied to other parts of the body throughout the world, for spinal injuries of the neck, for instance, and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Doctor, would that be coming a time where despite being in traction a cast would be applied during the time of the traction or when is the time that a plaster cast would be applied to the patient?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A plaster cast is placed when an X-ray control and a clinical check-up, of course, shows that the bones -- bone elements are in a correct position. That is when the second phase of the treatment is applied with rigid plaster immobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the patient still during traction in a plaster cast or only after the traction cease to be applied or weights cease to be applied?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While the leg is being extended with the help of traction a plaster bandage is placed and then a final X-ray check-up is made and only then is traction removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So some form of cast, as I understand you, is already applied while the patient is still under traction; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just for the few minutes, until the plaster sets and we maintain the correct position of the bones with the help of the plaster. So I'm talking about minutes. After that, the need and importance of traction ceases. There's no need for it any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
